conservation.notes: Has the second-greatest mortality of any bat species from wind turbines, after the hoary bat, through barotrauma. Documented to carry the fungus that causes white-nose syndrome, though no individuals have been seen with clinical symptoms.

human_tolerance.notes: Widespread across the whole eastern half of the continent, right into cities, and the IUCN records that it tolerates some habitat disturbance. It roosts by hanging in foliage and in leaf piles, so a garden with mature trees and moths overhead suits it, though it is killed in numbers by cars, tall buildings and wind turbines.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The breeding season starts in the autumn, and more than one male can sire a single litter.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Pups are born between May and July, most commonly as a group of three and occasionally up to five; the female has four nipples and can nourish several at once. The pups learn to fly about a month after being born and are weaned then, but stay with the mother for a while before roosting alone.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Ohio is inside this species' spring and summer range, the Great Lakes and Great Plains region; in winter it occurs in the southeastern United States and northeastern Mexico, with the greatest concentrations in coastal areas. The US-OH activity curve this record carries agrees: it is near zero in November, December, January and February and rises through March and April.

vocalizations.description: The ultrasonic clicks the bat emits through its mouth or nose while flying and hunting. Microbats use their larynx to emit the signals, and because they rely on echolocation to search for prey they make little use of smell while foraging. The call is far above human hearing, so the simulation renders it as a very quiet, very frequent buzz, which is the audible shadow of a click train rather than the click train itself.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 5218543 and family Vespertilionidae from the GBIF Backbone record for the accepted name; iNaturalist taxon id 40522 from the iNaturalist taxa API; ITIS TSN 180016 from the ITISWebService scientific-name search, which returns Lasiurus borealis (Muller, 1776) as an exact match; Wikidata Q301708 from a Wikidata entity search for the scientific name.

conservation.note: IUCN category from Wikidata P141, which points at the IUCN 'Least Concern' item; the article spells out the criteria and the two named threats, wind-turbine barotrauma and white-nose syndrome without clinical cases.

range.note: 'The eastern red bat is widely distributed in eastern North America and Bermuda. It generally occurs east of the Continental Divide, including southern Canada and northeastern Mexico.' The populations formerly included from the western United States, Central America and northern South America have been reassigned to the desert red bat and are deliberately excluded.

traits.limb_count.note: Four, because a bat is a mammal with two forelimbs modified as wings and two hind limbs. The biped_winged mesh plan is the only flying plan in the kit and it draws the two hind legs, which is why the two counts differ; this is noted so the mismatch does not read as an error.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'Its wings are long and pointed' and the species 'hunt[s] insects in flight ... and may catch an insect in mid-air directly with the mouth or use their tail membranes or wings'; it hangs and moves about in foliage by day, so Climb, Fly and Glide are the modes.

traits.thermoregulation.note: A mammal, and the Bat article notes that temperate species which enter hibernation or torpor are heterothermic, so the correct value is Endotherm with the seasonal strategy carrying the torpor.

traits.skin.note: 'Its entire body is densely furred, including its uropatagium', with back hairs about 5.8 mm and uropatagium hairs 2.6 mm.

traits.perching.note: A bat hangs by its feet and climbs about in foliage and leaf piles, so perching is true. The mesh's 'perched' pose stands in for the hanging roost.

traits.nest_type.note: None: this species builds no nest. Pups are born in the autumn breeding season and carried, then hang in foliage and hide in leaf piles rather than in any constructed nest, so the schema's None is the accurate value rather than a cavity or a platform.

traits.length_m.note: 'measuring 109 mm (4.3 in) from head to tail', used directly. The tail is 52.7 mm of that, which is where the 0.5 tail_ratio in look.proportions comes from, and the forearm is about 40.6 mm.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Allen Kurta argues that the lifespan for an eastern red bat is about two years, although they can probably live even longer.' The attributed estimate of about two years is what is recorded.

traits.diet.note: 'Eastern red bats are insectivorous, preying heavily on moths, with other insect taxa also consumed', and the Bat article names this species among the bats that 'hunt insects in flight'. One food type, so the diet is entirely invertebrate.

traits.social.note: 'eastern red bats have on average three pups at a time, and some eastern red bats have given birth to as many as five pups', with four nipples, and the pups 'remain with their mother for a while before roosting on their own'. The Bat article's contrast, that the hoary bat 'is mostly solitary, aside from mothers with young', describes the same pattern for a close relative. Group, with the band set to the documented maximum family size of five.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Most bats are nocturnal, and many roost in caves or other refuges', and 'Bats are usually nocturnal but are known to exhibit diurnal behaviour in temperate regions during summer to make up for insufficient nighttime feeding'. The named species is a microbat, i.e. one of the echolocating majority, so Nocturnal is recorded.

traits.defense.note: 'Eastern red bats are often attacked and killed by hawks and owls, or aggressive species like blue jays and crows', with hawks the major predator of bats hiding in leaf piles, and the Bat article's account of bats evolving nocturnality 'to avoid predators'. There is no display or chemical defence in either source, so escape by flight is the whole of the recorded behaviour: Flee.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement at 0.45, and deliberately in the middle: the IUCN criteria say it 'tolerates some habitat disturbance' and it ranges across the whole eastern half of the continent including cities, but it hides in leaf piles by day and is taken in numbers by hawks, owls, jays and crows. It is neither habituated nor bold.

habitat.use.note: 'Species that hunt insects in flight ... may catch an insect in mid-air directly with the mouth', and 'Bats in flight make vocal signals for traffic control'; the animal spends its night on the wing and its day hanging in foliage and leaf piles, so aerial takes 0.8 and arboreal 0.2.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: The article records hawks as 'a major predator for bats hiding in leaf piles', which is this species' daytime resting place, so leaf_litter is the site it depends on and is therefore the shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: The moth-and-insect diet for the single feeding tag, the leaf-pile hiding place for `leaf_litter`, and the roosting sentence for `shelter` and `perch`. No `water` resource is declared: the cited sources record no drinking behaviour for this species, so the drink branch of the behaviour program stays inactive rather than the record asserting something unsourced.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: The IUCN criteria in the article say it 'tolerates some habitat disturbance', and the range covers the densely settled eastern seaboard and the Great Lakes. `uses_gardens` follows from a garden that has mature trees to hang in and moths overhead; the numeric tolerances are omitted because neither source gives an artificial-light, imperviousness or road-mortality figure for bats, and inventing one would be worse than the gap.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'In the spring and summer, it can be found in the Great Lakes region and the Great Plains region' against 'In the winter, it occurs in the southeastern United States and northeastern Mexico': the species leaves the Great Lakes for the southeast, and the Bat article describes exactly this for a long-distance migrant, that it 'may fly at night and go into a torpid state roosting in the daytime' because 'nocturnal bats have a conflict between travelling and eating'. Migration, and no winter_fraction because the schema reserves that field for PartialMigration.

seasonal.phases.note: The autumn breeding season, the May-to-July pups and the one-month-to-fly period, and the split between the Great Lakes summer range and the southeastern winter range all come from the article; the month boundaries are judgements aligned to those statements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'Eastern red bat pups learn to fly about a month after being born, after which they are weaned', which gives duration_days 30. There is no egg stage because a bat gives live birth. scale 0.4 is a judgement: the article gives no pup weight, and the Bat article's note that 'A newborn bat pup can be up to 40 percent of the mother's weight' is about a maximum in other species, so the pup is drawn at about 40% rather than at the 10% a linear 10 g-against-100 g ratio would give.

vocalizations.echolocate.note: 'Microbats use their larynx to emit echolocation signals through the mouth or the nose' and 'Insectivorous bats have less use for smell during foraging, as they rely on echolocation to search for prey'; the Bat article also records that 'In addition to echolocating prey, bat ears are sensitive to sounds made by their prey, such as the fluttering of moth wings', which is the prey this species takes. The species' own article does not describe the call, so this entry is sourced to the Bat article and marked Buzz, the schema's term for a continuous ultrasonic call. The seconds-long cooldown stands in for the hundreds of clicks per second a real click train carries; no recording is cited, because an open recording of a microbat's ultrasonic output would be a different thing from this.

look.note: 'males being brick or rusty red, and females being a slightly more frosted shade of red. Both male and female eastern red bats have distinctive shoulder patches of white fur' with 'Fur on its ventral surface ... usually lighter in color', 'Its ears are short and rounded, with triangular tragi' and 'Its wings are long and pointed'. The white shoulder patches are drawn as extra parts on the wings because both sexes have them and they are the field mark. wing_aspect is set well above the other flying birds here, at 4.2, from the article's own reading of 'The aspect ratio and wing loading of eastern red bat wings indicates that they fly relatively quickly and are moderately maneuverable'; the remaining proportions are authored from the 109 mm head-to-tail length, the 52.7 mm tail and the short rounded ears.

behavior.note: This species ships its own program, species/lasiurus-borealis/behavior.json (fsm-aerial-insectivore-v1), because no shared program fits it. fsm-ground-forager-v1 and fsm-anuran-nocturnal-v1 have no flight gait at all; bt-perching-songbird-v1 needs a song and an alarm call and ends every branch in perch_nearest, which is not how a bat moves; fsm-seabird-predator-v1 hunts a hard-coded small_vertebrate tag while walking and adds a carrion state, and this bat takes insects in the air. The program roosts the animal by day, launches after dark on hunger or opportunistically, alternates patrol and echolocation, takes invertebrates in flight, and drops clear of a threat - which is what 'Eastern red bats are often attacked and killed by hawks and owls' and 'Heterothermic bats ... go into a torpid state roosting in the daytime' describe. insect_m is 80 m because bats can travel significant distances each night; flee_m is 25 m, longer than any other mammal here, because a bat's escape is a high-speed aerial one rather than a sprint.

traits.wingspan_m.note: The article gives no wingspan for this species, so it is derived from the one wing measurement it does give: 'Its forearm is approximately 40.6 mm (1.60 in) long.' A bat's wing membrane spans from the shoulder along the forearm and finger bones out to the hind limb on each side, so the total span is a little over twice the forearm length; twice 40.6 mm is 81.2 mm and the membrane's own width and the body's breadth add the rest, giving 0.095 m. This is a morphometric estimate, not a reported measurement, and is the weakest of the numeric fields in this record.

activity.US-OH.note: Curve from tools/fetch_activity.py at its default min_obs of 300. This is the one record in the oh-sandusky set whose US-OH curve lands on a tier-C, non-commercial source: the species has only 359 GBIF records and 284 iNaturalist observations in Ohio in total, all licences, so neither dataset clears the observation floor for a strictly CC0/CC-BY tier A curve and fetch_activity.py had to fall back to the CC-BY-NC records to build anything at all. Running the fetcher with --min-obs 200 pulls iNaturalist in as a second tier-C source, which was tested and rejected: it doubles the number of tier-4 sources the maintainers would have to isolate later, for a curve that changes the twelve monthly values very little. The shape is robust either way - near zero from November to February, peaking in July - and it agrees with the winter range in seasonal.phases.
